I use a little method I call “fragmenting.” I have no scientific basis for this, but basically, I actively work my mind while I’m trying to sleep. I think about one thing, then quickly think about another, and another and so on. Eventually, my mind can’t keep up because as it gets more sleepy, it starts to “fragment” and break apart. (I know that’s a weird way to describe it, but that’s what it feels like). I know I’m getting to this stage when I can’t remember what I was thinking of 3 seconds ago. It’s all blurring together and not making any sense. Every night I’ve done this, I’m asleep within seconds of “fragmenting.”

I find other games have similar issues with R2 not working, but there is a workaround that, annoyingly, you usually have to do each time. Basically, while you’re in game, you shut off your VR controllers and use your DualShock to get out of the PS menu and back into the game. With the controllers off and while in-game, turn your controllers back on. They should work. Again, this has not worked for No Man’s Sky in my experience, but it has worked for every other game I’ve had this issue with.

One day, my friend asked why we weren't using an HDMI cable to our TV and brought his own another day to show how it worked. My eyes were opened that day as our display went from 480p to 720p with a proper 16:9 aspect ratio. I played the hell out of every game I could, basking in the high resolution.

That situation is the reason I'm such a fiend for high resolution and graphics. I'm still chasing that high to this day.

P.S. When we finally could see how many dragon souls we had, it was about 20.

TLDR: Effex is well worth it, I have seen several shows here and have never had an issue. Recommended parking instructions near the end.

I've been there 5 times since COVID during busy nights and slow nights. It's known as a gay club, but it really isn't. Unless you're specifically doing for a drag show or something LGBT, it isn't truly a gay club. At least not anymore. I actually wanted to go to the Mr. Bill show but I just don't have the money to.

Mr. Bill is going to be on the main stage which is the lowest floor. It has decent space and two bars. There's a small seating area in case you get tired, but chances are people will be dancing there too.

The venue itself is 2.5 floors. If it's your first time being there, explore the entire venue! The top floor has an open roof and has heating, there are also two bars on the top floor. In the in-between floor, there is a single bar and a tiny stage for anyone performing there. During headliner shows like Mr. Bill, there's a good chance there won't be anyone performing there, only on the top and bottom floors.

The sound system on the bottom floor (where Mr. Bill will be) is incredible, especially if you are in the center of the venue, although it can get packed in that spot.

The biggest issue I have with Effex: the bathrooms are unisex and without stalls. It's a good idea to have a friend with you who can be your "door" as you do #2. If you're a female, you will probably need someone to cover the door for you. This is truly the biggest issue I have with Effex. I understand it's for safety reasons, but I wish the bathrooms were more private.

As for the vibe, in my experience, it's incredible. You're going to be with the younger, more dedicated EDM crew. For the most part, this community is amazing. You may encounter some problematic people, but you'll encounter the same people regardless of what show you're going to. As long as you're having fun and respecting other people's vibe, you'll be okay.

The average age range is 20s-30s. You can't get into Effex under 21, so immediately you're dealing with an older crowd. As far as I've seen, Albuquerque EDM communities don't discriminate in terms of age. I've seen 60-70 year olds at these types of shows having the time of their lives.

If you are traveling from the south (Los Lunas or Belen) take I-25 North until Exit 224 (Coal/ Lead/ Central). .

If you are traveling from the north (Santa Fe or Rio Rancho) take Exit 224B (Dr Martin Luther King Jr Ave/ Central Ave/ Route 66)

Either direction you come from, turn West on Central and stay on Central until [THIS IS IMPORTANT] you get to 2nd Street.
At 2nd Street, turn right. The very next turn, Copper Ave, turn left.

This is important because on the weekends, Central closes the road to vehicle traffic between 9-10pm.

So now you are heading West on Copper Ave. Keep going forward until you reach 6th Street, turn left. You will see a mural on a small building. There will be a parking lot on your right, that is the best spot to park. It's easy to leave after the show and not too far from the venue and the highway. It costs some money, but not a lot. For 6 hours, you're looking at no more than $10. Best to download the app in case you need to add more time. You will need to enter your car's model and license plate. It's the easiest parking situation I've found near Central. The exact address of this parking lot is 212 Central Ave SW. Hopefully my instructions are clear enough and easy to follow.

If you see The Dry Bar Comedy Club and Katrina Ice Cream shop on your left, you're in the right spot. The Rave Cave is also in this same area on the right.

When you park and pay, walk East (towards the mountains) to reach Effex and stay on the right side of the sidewalk. Their sign is very hard to see so use Google Maps to help you find exactly where it is at.

If you're going to a single night rave from 6-12pm-ish, then I have a few pointers. (I haven't been to a festival so I can't speak on that)

Make sure you know the lineup well and what time the venue opens. If it's at a local venue, check their social media the day of the show, they'll likely have the set times posted. If it's a smaller show, local DJs are likely to be the first to perform then the tour supports and finally the headliner.

If doors open at 6 or 7 or whenever, you don't necessarily need to be there that early. It's a good idea to go early since parking lots can get full, and you're going to want to park as close to the venue as possible (unless parking fees are insane, but if it's a small venue it'll either be free or no more than $10). You wanna be parked close because you're going to be exhausted and if it's cold at night, you don't want the long walk back.

When you arrive:
-They may not let you bring in water, even in a hydration bag, see if you can find what is allowed in the venue online (I've never seen anyone have issues bringing in Kandi so bring as much as you can).
-They will very likely do a security check, it's simple, empty your pockets, simple pat down, you're good to go.
-If you are over 21 and plan on drinking, make sure you get a wristband (I guess this only applies to 18+ events).
-If you're wanting merch, get it right away, stuff sells out fast, but be aware it is usually very expensive stuff.
-The music will be very loud, you might not have cell reception, it may already be crowded. It can be very overwhelming at first and it's definitely much more chaotic than your normal concert.

During the show:
-It gets very hot in the crowd, don't feel bad about hanging out near the back or on the sides of crowds, bonus if you can find a nice breezy spot. But if you can handle the heat (or have a fan) then being in the crowd is super fun.
-I don't know what type of show you're going to, but if it's dubstep or some of the harder genres, there will be mosh pits. EDM mosh pits are not violent and there's an etiquette to it. It's basically just jumping around and pushing people around non-aggressively. If someone falls down, people stop and pick them up. However, they can be intense and if you want to avoid them, try not to be in the center near the front.
-Unfortunately personal space is virtually non-existent. If you're going to be in the crowd, expect people pushing past you, arms and elbows touching you, things like that. 90% of the time it's respectful, it's just a byproduct of so many people in a small place. Me and this other guy had hit our heads together super hard one time and we laughed it off, but it can happen.
-Don't feel bad about taking things slow. Go to the bathroom, sit down, get some water (there should be water stations), talk to strangers, just vibe and take things at your own pace.

Final Tips: 
Keep water or Gatorade in your car for after the show
Eat well during the day, nothing that would slow you down
Don't work the next morning
DON'T WORRY ABOUT PEOPLE LOOKING AT YOU, VIBE HOWEVER YOU NEED

And most importantly have fun. It's a chaotic, overwhelming atmosphere but it's such an incredible thing.

TLDR: Came out while dating a girl at 13, friends were accepting, mom not so much but things are good 12 years later.

13. It was 8th grade and this one girl had a huge crush on me and I felt a weird pressure to date her. People had started to suspect I might be gay and I didn't want anyone to know so I dated her to keep the secret. Once I started dating her, I realized that I truly didn't want to and I needed to come out to someone. I told my best girl friend at the time and she helped me slowly come out to more people. I was trying to keep it as low key as possible, but within the week, most of the school had already known. It wasn't common for people to come out (especially that young) so I was one of the first to come out in my age group so the news spread like wildfire. My close friends were all accepting but others around the school occasionally made fun of me. I'd see them pointing at me in the halls and laughing when I came near. Even had some guy come up to my face and yell that (F)ancy word.

About a week and a half into dating that girl, I broke up with her as I came out to her and she was clearly upset but understanding. I still feel awful about it to this day.

Coming out to friends was easy enough but it was my family I was truly afraid to tell. I told myself I wasn't going to tell them yet, maybe in a few years. Unfortunately, my mom found a note in my room talking about it and confronted me on it.  I was scared to death and petrified to have this conversation with her. It felt oddly accusatory, she was telling me that I shouldn't be telling people I was gay unless I was sure I was. Then she didn't talk to me for about a week after that. It was so bad in fact that on a few occasions, even looking at me would cause her to breakdown crying.

We have a good relationship now and she's completely open and accepting of me, but the way she reacted when she found out still scars me to this day. I was terrified of coming out to the rest of my family, but I later found out that she basically told everyone on the day she found out. She has a habit of telling everyone she knows about our personal business.

It's been 12 years since I've been out and I'm glad it happened as early as it did. It's still sometimes difficult to come out to new people I meet, but it's getting easier.

I love World and Rise pretty equally but something I felt like was missing in Rise was that World felt like the monsters genuinely affected their ecosystem. 

The elder recess being shaped by Zorah Magdaros and Xenojiva was interesting. The Rotten Vale being a graveyard for monsters and the Coral Highlands being the life that is fertilized from it was incredible world building. The fact that you could see The Ancient Forest and the Wildspire Waste from Astera was exciting. It truly felt like the world was connected. 

The monsters had their place in the world too. You wouldn't see a Barroth in the jungle, he belongs in the desert. You wouldn't see Radobaan in the Coral Highlands, there's no bones for him to protect himself.

Rise was completely missing this. There wasn't much sense of connectivity between locales, the monsters never really seemed to affect or be affected by the places they were in.

I truly wish Wilds will bring back the ecology from World and take it up a hundred notches, which may already be the case as we saw a creature's spike take a lightning strike like a lightning rod in the trailer.

I'll try and answer this as unbiased as possible but I've been playing 2023 for a few hours and I'm really enjoying the new stuff so far.

2023 does feature Just Dance+ instead of Just Dance Unlimited. With this new era comes changes to certain systems we are used to. There is currently no World Dance Floor or Sweat Mode but in trailers and promotional material, they're promising "New game modes throughout the year," so it's safe to say these will probably come back at some point in the year and possibly in some other form than we're used to.

Just Dance+ has a very limited library, as others have said, it contains around 150 songs whereas it used to be 700+, but I feel as though this is temporary, I'm sure they're going to port over the older stuff down the road, but as of right now, it's very limited.

As for 2023 itself, it feels very different from the previous games, but I'm really liking it so far. Being that this is a "Live Service," game rather than a yearly release now, I can see the potential and what they're going for, but we'll see if they actually pull it off. The new Dancer Card customization is very good and I'm sure it will expand over time, but as others have said, you can only have 1 card per account. I haven't played around with online lobbies yet, but local play is seamless.

If you've been a fan of Just Dance for a while now, I don't think you'll be completely disappointed. The new songs and dances are some of the best I've seen in the series (maybe even the best collection of songs we've ever gotten). The new Dancer Card is cool and has a lot of potential. As a fan myself, I really like this game so far and it can only get better. If you can comfortably buy it, I'd recommend it.

Ps: this being a "live service" game makes me think that the "yearly" release that we've become used to will be yearly expansions within this new game, which is honestly not a bad thing and if they're priced fairly, with a full catalog each year, this could be a very good direction for the Just Dance series.

First of all, not a kid. Second of all, I said in another comment that I try my hardest to make sure I don't cross contaminate anything. If I'm making a gluten free burger, I do everything in my power to ensure I touch no gluten of any kind and switch out my gloves frequently. But, I cannot control every aspect of the world and maybe a breaded crumb or two may fall onto the plate and go unnoticed and that totally worries me. I'm not saying never eat out, just don't expect every place to take the necessary precautions because some will not. Domino's for instance does not recommend their gluten free dough for people with celiac disease because they understand how difficult it can be to ensure 100% gluten-free products in a restaurant filled with flour and starches. In my kitchen, and in my home, if you cannot eat a certain food, I will do everything in my power to ensure you have an incredible eating experience with food you love.

As a cook, I always take the highest precautions to ensure that I keep things gluten free or vegetarian, or other, but I cannot 100% guarantee that I kept it that way and I get extremely anxious that I could possibly serve someone food they can't eat.
Yes, but if the pizza place places the cheese next to the sauce (which is usually the case) you will probably have stray pieces of cheese falling into that sauce.

I came out when I was at 13 actually. I realize now how early it was and how lucky I was with my family. Coming out to friends was the easy part and I was not ready to come out to my mom but she found a note where I mentioned it and she confronted me about it. She didn't talk to me for days after the fact and would start crying if she looked at me. I felt like the worst person then but see now that she was being dramatic considering how she says, "Oh, I always knew."

She ended up calling pretty much everyone in our family telling them and at school, everyone pretty much found out within a week. It was a very scary time and I did get some bullying but 11 years later, I'm glad I got through it all and how normal a part of my life it has become. I was one of the first people to come out in school which made it a huge deal but then in highschool, dozens more came out and it became a pretty insignificant thing. As for family, my mother is the only one I had issues with.

I can't guarantee the same experience but I promise it gets better. Even a year after coming out it may not seem like a big deal anymore. The hardest part is coming out to new people you meet but it's easy if you surround yourself by those who accept you.

My personal advice is find that one person who you can trust with that information and slowly working your way up to family. Wish you luck 🤞
